Flight-tracking analysis · Nov. 13, 2026

On Nov. 13, departures from U.S. airports stopped almost all at once at 12:38 p.m. Pacific, 16 minutes before the FAA's nationwide ground stop officially took effect, and the sky slowly emptied. When the stop was lifted at 5:15 p.m., departures took 21 more minutes to restart.

Data: adsb.lol open ADS-B network · data through 10:29 p.m. PT · Each plane inside the title stands for aircraft in the air, from 10 a.m. (left) to the latest data (right)

The bold lines are Nov. 13; the faint lines show the same hours on Nov. 12 (dashed) and on Nov. 6, a normal Friday (dotted). Departures always thin out late in the evening, so compare the bold line with the faint ones, not with its own afternoon. At 12:38 p.m. Pacific, departures fell off a cliff. The number of aircraft in the air drained for hours as flights already aloft landed, bottoming out at 475 at 5:42 p.m.. After the FAA lifted the stop at 5:15 p.m., departures surged, briefly overshot and then settled well below normal; Part 3 explains why. This page tells it in three parts: how the sky emptied, what kept flying when it was nearly empty, and how it came back.

Part 1
The stop
Departures halt, and the sky drains

Just after 12:38 p.m. Pacific time on Friday, the steady stream of departures from American airports stopped. For the half hour before, about 30 airline flights took off every minute, much like the same hour a day earlier. Within two minutes, the rate had dropped to a handful, and it stayed there: 2 a minute on average over the following half hour. The Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop, which the agency attributed to a telecommunications outage affecting air traffic control, took effect at 2:54 p.m. Central (12:54 p.m. Pacific), according to News9. Public flight-tracking data shows the departures stopped 16 minutes before that. Nothing new was going up. The flights already in the air carried on to their destinations, and the number of aircraft over the country fell steadily, from 6,552 at the moment of the collapse to 475 at the low point, 5:42 p.m. Pacific. A day earlier at the same time, 4,602 aircraft were airborne.

The cliff came first

Counting airline takeoffs minute by minute makes the timing plain. The rate did not taper off as you might expect if airlines were holding flights at the gate one by one. It fell off a cliff, from about 30 a minute to 2, between 12:38 p.m. and 12:40 p.m.. The official ground-stop time comes 16 minutes later, in the shaded gap below. Early reports cited the 2:54 p.m. Central time. The data suggests departures were already being held in practice before the formal nationwide order. One possibility is that facilities hit by the communications outage stopped releasing flights on their own first. We could not find an official FAA timeline that settles it.

Where it started

Airline sources told CNN that the failure began with network routers at Chicago's Midway airport and spread nationwide (CNN). The tracking data points to Chicago too. At O'Hare, departures stopped at 12:16 p.m. Pacific (2:16 in Chicago), 22 minutes before the nationwide collapse and 38 minutes before the FAA's order. By the time departures stopped everywhere, O'Hare would normally have sent off about 58 more airline flights. It sent none. Midway itself is too small to time precisely: its last departure was at 12:31 p.m., a few minutes ahead of most airports. It was not one airline pausing: United, American, their regional partners and foreign carriers all stopped at O'Hare at once, while Southwest, United, American and Delta kept departing elsewhere at normal rates until about 12:35. That pattern fits a problem in Chicago's air traffic control. Then it reached everyone else within minutes. Half of the 25 busiest airports sent off their last departure between 12:34 p.m. and 12:37 p.m.. The map below shows when each one went quiet.

data.text/html:
Then everywhere at once

Outside Chicago, there was little sign of a wave rolling across the country. Splitting departures into rough time-zone bands finds the collapse at 12:36 p.m. in the East, 12:38 p.m. in the Central band, 12:38 p.m. in the Mountain band and 12:38 p.m. in the West (all Pacific time). At the biggest hubs, the half hour after the cliff looked like an airport closed for the night.

data.text/html:
Landings kept coming

Takeoffs and landings normally track each other closely. That's how the number of aircraft aloft stays roughly level through the afternoon. After 12:38 p.m. the two lines split: takeoffs dropped to near zero, while landings continued at close to their usual pace as flights already en route reached their destinations. The gap between the lines is the sky draining.

data.text/html:
The middle of the sky emptied first

Sorting airborne aircraft by altitude shows the order the sky emptied in. The layers between 15,000 and 35,000 feet, where jets climb out after takeoff, thinned fastest because nothing new was climbing through them. Two layers held up longer: cruise altitudes above 35,000 feet, where long flights already en route kept going, and the lowest band under 5,000 feet, which is mostly small private planes and helicopters.

An empty state

One moment on the map sums it up. At 4:28 p.m. Pacific, not a single aircraft was visible in the sky over Wyoming. At noon there had been 36. At the same time a day earlier there were 24. Receiver coverage is thin at low altitude over the rural West, so a small plane flying low could be missed. The jets at cruise altitude that normally cross the state all day are hard to miss.

Replay the day

Every aircraft broadcasting its position over the U.S., one frame per minute, from 10 a.m. to 10:29 p.m. Pacific. The map opens at the low point. Drag the slider back to 12:38 p.m. to watch departures stop, to 4:28 p.m. to see Wyoming empty, and past 5:15 p.m. to watch the sky refill. Aircraft are colored by altitude; grey ones are on the ground with transponders on. Canadian and Mexican traffic is faded. Hover over a plane for its callsign and type.

Part 2
At the bottom
What kept flying, and what didn't

Who kept flying

Airline traffic fell furthest, and the mix of what stayed aloft shows it. At the low point, 5:42 p.m. Pacific, compared with the same time a day earlier, airborne traffic by category stood at: helicopter 44%, general aviation 19%, other 19%, business jet 11%, airline 6%. Helicopters (police, medical, news) and small private planes made up a growing share of what was still flying.

Below 18,000 feet, pilots can fly under visual flight rules without clearances from the en-route centers that were failing, a point also made in a parallel analysis of the same data. Business jets show it. Only 37 took off from lower-48 airports during the stop, against 235 in the same hours a day earlier, and those that flew stayed lower: 34% of their positions were above 18,000 feet, against 57% normally. Small propeller planes, which rarely climb that high anyway (3% vs. 5%), carried on much as usual.

Two states kept flying

Alaska Airlines said in a statement that flights within Alaska and inter-island flights in Hawaii were not affected by the ground stop, The New York Times reported. The tracking data agrees. Between 12:38 p.m. and the lift, airline departures in Alaska ran at 82% of the previous day's level for the same hours and Hawaii at 91%. In the lower 48 states the figure was 4%. Hawaiian Airlines' Boeing 717s kept shuttling between the islands, and international flights by Japan Airlines, ANA, Korean Air, Qantas and Philippine Airlines kept leaving Honolulu. In Alaska, Alaska Airlines' in-state jets, regional carriers such as Bering Air and Ravn, and the cargo flights that stop in Anchorage kept flying.

data.text/html:
Long-haul flights got out

The halt was not total. Some international flights were departing U.S. airports, including Honolulu and San Francisco for Asia, and several left Kennedy for Europe, The New York Times reported. The FAA had not said which international flights were cleared to go. Wikipedia's account of the day says Pacific-bound flights from San Francisco were cleared about two hours after the advisory, and some transatlantic flights from the East Coast were allowed to leave. The data shows them clearly in the wide-body jets that fly long international routes. In the hour after the collapse, just 1 wide-body left mainland airports, against 91 the day before. Then they started coming back: from about 3:30 p.m. Pacific, the evening bank of flights to Europe and Asia began to leave. In the latest hour of data, 81 departed, about the usual number, led by New York, Miami, Los Angeles, Newark and San Francisco. Since the collapse, 668 wide-bodies have left the lower 48.

Where the flights left from mattered. A long-haul flight from a coastal gateway reaches oceanic airspace within minutes. Oceanic airspace is managed through a separate, largely text-based system, as the head of the air traffic controllers' union explained on CNN. A flight from an inland hub first has to cross the en-route centers that were failing. During the stop, coastal gateways sent off 55% of their usual wide-body departures (JFK 22 vs. 19, IAD 17 vs. 20, EWR 15 vs. 22), and inland hubs 15%; DFW, IAH, DEN, CLT sent none. Those long-haul flights, plus flights within Alaska and Hawaii, kept the departure line in the chart at the top of the page off zero: of the 496 airline departures from U.S. airports during the stop, 37% were in Alaska or Hawaii and 26% were wide-bodies from the lower 48.

data.text/html:
The neighbors stopped flying to the U.S.

The FAA controls only U.S. airspace, but the stop reached across both borders. Canadian airports suspended U.S.-bound flights while domestic Canadian flights carried on, Global News reported. And the FAA asked Mexico's federal aviation agency to keep all aircraft at Mexican airports with scheduled flights to the United States on the ground, the Mexican agency said, according to The New York Times. The data shows the same split. Departures from Canadian airports that went on to enter U.S. airspace fell from about 28 per half hour to 7, while flights that stayed out of the U.S. ran at 104% of the previous day's level. Mexico points the same way, with far fewer flights in the data: U.S.-bound departures went from 6 to 1 per half hour, and other flights ran at 106% of normal. The volunteer receivers that feed this data cover far less of Mexico than of the U.S. and Canada, so the Mexican numbers are small.

data.text/html:
Where the planes piled up

With nothing taking off and flights still landing, airports filled up. Airlines warned that some were running out of gates and taxiway space, and one airline source told CNN that Austin might be the first to saturate (CNN). Counting aircraft on the ground with their transponders on (mostly planes taxiing or waiting, since parked planes often switch theirs off) shows modest build-ups rather than dramatic ones. The largest were at MCO (2.4 times its morning level), DFW (2.4 times its morning level), JFK (1.5 times its morning level). Austin was at 0.7 times its morning level, so it does not stand out in this data. This measure is noisy: it depends on which receivers can hear aircraft on the ground at each airport.

Part 3
The return
The ban is lifted and the sky refills

The lift

The FAA lifted the nationwide ground stop at 8:15 p.m. Eastern (5:15 p.m. Pacific), Al Jazeera reported, after about four hours and 20 minutes. The sky did not refill at once. Departures stayed at the ground-stop trickle for about 21 minutes and only began climbing at 5:36 p.m., the mirror image of the afternoon, when departures stopped 16 minutes before the order. The East came back first, at 5:10 p.m., 5 minutes before the lift was announced; 13 of its first 26 airline departures were wide-bodies, the jets used on long international routes. Then the West (5:33 p.m.), the central states (5:42 p.m.) and the mountain states (6:20 p.m.). By 10:29 p.m. Pacific, the latest data, airline departures were running at 85% of the previous day's level and the number of aircraft in the air at 98%. Airlines warned that delays and cancellations would continue as they got aircraft and crews back into position.

Why departures overshot, then settled

After the restart, departures climbed quickly, peaked around 7:15 p.m. and then fell back. Matching flight numbers against a normal Friday, Nov. 6, explains the shape. About 46% of the airline departures after the lift were flights that normally leave during the afternoon: the held backlog, released in a wave. Underneath it, the regular evening schedule was thin. Only about 9% of the flights that normally leave between 5:15 p.m. and 9:59 p.m. left within an hour of their usual time. As the backlog drained, departures settled at that lower level.

What happened to the afternoon's flights

The flight-tracking data has no airline schedules, so this section uses a normal Friday as a stand-in: a flight number that left at 2:10 p.m. on Nov. 6 is treated as scheduled for about 2:10 p.m. on Nov. 13, and then looked for on Nov. 13. It is an estimate. Schedules change from week to week, and some flights are missing from the data. On the normal morning of Nov. 13, before the stop, 57% of flight numbers left within 15 minutes of their Nov. 6 time and 27% were not seen at all. That is the noise floor for the numbers below. Of the 6,766 flights "scheduled" to leave lower-48 airports during the stop, 1,360 left later, a median 4.4 hours late. 5,406 had not been seen departing by 10:29 p.m. Pacific. Allowing for the normal-morning noise floor, that suggests roughly 3,566 of them were cancelled or still waiting. For the whole day, Cirium counted more than 8,200 cancelled flights, over 31% of Friday's U.S. schedule (The New York Times). For the evening after the lift, only 16% of scheduled flight numbers had been seen departing by 10:29 p.m. Pacific.

In context
How rare is this?
Nationwide ground stops, from 9/11 to today

Nationwide ground stops are rare. By Wikipedia's count, Nov. 13 was only the third in U.S. history; some outlets counted it as the second since 9/11.
Date What happened What stopped How long
Sept. 11, 2001 Terrorist hijackings All civil traffic: departures halted, and every aircraft in the air ordered to land About two days; commercial flights resumed Sept. 13
Jan. 11, 2023 Failure of the NOTAM system that publishes safety notices to pilots, after a contractor deleted files Domestic departures About 1.5 hours, until 9 a.m. Eastern
Nov. 13, 2026 Communications failure affecting the FAA's en-route control centers Departures, with exceptions for Alaska, Hawaii and some international flights About 4 hours 20 minutes, 3:54 to 8:15 p.m. Eastern
The first was different in kind. After the hijackings on Sept. 11, 2001, controllers brought down every aircraft in the sky: 4,638 commercial and private planes were landed and accounted for within about three hours. The second, on Jan. 11, 2023, halted domestic departures for about an hour and a half while the FAA restored the NOTAM system. Friday's stop sat between the two. Like 2023, it halted departures and let flights already aloft finish their trips. But it lasted more than twice as long, and it was declared in the middle of a busy afternoon rather than early in the morning. Its cause, a communications failure affecting the en-route centers that handle aircraft at cruise altitude, was still under investigation. Smaller, airline-specific stops have become more common. Carriers asked the FAA to hold their own fleets after technology failures at United in September 2023, at American, Delta, United and Allegiant during the CrowdStrike outage of July 2024, at American on Christmas Eve 2024, and twice at Alaska Airlines in 2025. Sources: Wikipedia: 2026 US ground stop · Wikipedia: 2023 FAA system outage · Every US nationwide ground stop, from 9/11 to today · NPR on the 2023 outage · Snopes on "first since 9/11"

Data

Positions come from adsb.lol, an open, unfiltered network of volunteer ADS-B receivers. It publishes a snapshot of every aircraft it hears every 10 seconds, in one file per half hour, usually 30 to 60 minutes after the half hour ends. This page downloads those files when it runs and keeps one position per aircraft per minute. Each position is assigned to the U.S., Canada or Mexico using Natural Earth borders, extended about 100 km offshore. "Over the U.S." includes Alaska and Hawaii. The page compares Nov. 13 with the same clock hours on Nov. 12. Aircraft types come from the tar1090 aircraft database.

Definitions

Takeoff: an aircraft's track goes from on the ground to airborne, or a track first appears in the air below 2,500 feet. Airline: an airline-style callsign (three-letter operator code plus flight number) on a jet or turboprop, or any medium or heavy jet. This includes regional and cargo carriers. Piston aircraft are excluded even with an operator code: flight schools such as the University of North Dakota fly under such codes, and their top-of-the-hour training departures otherwise look like an airline spike. Wide-body: Boeing 747/767/777/787, Airbus A330/A340/A350/A380 or MD-11, the aircraft used on most long international routes. Some fly domestic routes too. Wyoming: the state's borders are lines of latitude and longitude, so a box is its exact outline. Airport stop time: an airport's last airline departure before 12:53 p.m. Pacific (the collapse plus 15 minutes), shown only for airports where at least six departures would normally have left between that time and 12:53. Takeoffs are assigned to the nearest airport with scheduled service within about 10 km (OurAirports). Aircraft on the ground: positions reported as on the ground within about 4 km of an airport, every two minutes, compared with the same airport between 10 a.m. and 12:38 p.m. that day (receiver coverage at the ground differs a lot between days), smoothed with a 10-minute running median to remove brief bursts in the feed. Parked aircraft often switch transponders off, so this mostly counts aircraft taxiing or waiting. Airspace: simplified en-route center boundaries from the VATSpy data project, for illustration only. Cross-check: an independent analysis posted during the stop, using OpenSky Network and adsb.lol live data (post), counted 1,083, 1,035 and 990 aircraft airborne at 6:36, 6:42 and 6:49 p.m. Eastern; this data gives 1,060, 1,016 and 980 over the U.S. at the same moments, and the same airport counts within a few aircraft. That post describes all en-route centers failing at once; this data shows Chicago going quiet about 20 minutes before the rest of the country, and Alaska and Hawaii continuing to fly. Schedule estimate: there is no airline schedule in ADS-B data, so each U.S. airline flight number's departure time on Nov. 6 (a normal Friday) stands in for its schedule. Each Nov. 6 departure is matched to the first departure of the same flight number on Nov. 13 between 90 minutes early and 12 hours late (Nov. 6's own delays make some flights look early). Fractional and charter operators without fixed schedules are left out. Flight numbers come from the callsign the aircraft was broadcasting at the time. The shares on the normal morning of Nov. 13 show how noisy this is. Recovery time: the first minute, from half an hour before the lift, after which airline takeoffs run at at least twice the ground-stop rate for 20 minutes straight. Collapse time: the first minute after 11 a.m. Pacific when airline takeoffs over the next three minutes average less than 40% of the preceding half hour's rate. The same test is applied to each region. Into U.S. airspace: a departure from Canada or Mexico whose aircraft appears over the U.S. within four hours. This also catches some Canadian domestic routes that cut across U.S. airspace. Coverage of Mexico is much thinner than of the U.S. and Canada.

Caveats

Receiver coverage is incomplete, especially at low altitudes and in remote areas, so absolute counts are undercounts. The comparisons (before vs after, Nov. 13 vs Nov. 12) are more reliable than the totals. The 2:54 p.m. Central ground-stop time is as reported by News9; other outlets give only "Friday afternoon", and we could not find an official FAA timeline.

Reporting

CBS News · CNBC · CNN · News9 · The New York Times · Global News · Al Jazeera · NBC Washington · Wikipedia · CNN (live coverage) · CNN (origin and stranded passengers) · parallel ADS-B analysis
This report is a marimo notebook (source). Every number and chart is computed from the data shown at the top of the page, from a fixed snapshot of the flight-tracking data.
